title: When work ends
hook: putting work down at the end of the day
tomorrow: on this path, is it okay to want money?

segments.voice: Yesterday: colleagues, duties both ways, a loop and not a ladder. But even a good loop needs the shift to end.

The shift ends at six. At nine, you're still answering a customer in your head who left hours ago. The body clocked out; the mind took the work home on its back. So how do you stop carrying it? The Buddha tells a story about a man who almost did exactly that, with a raft.
screen: `OFF AT SIX. STILL AT IT AT NINE.` → `WORK HOME ON YOUR BACK.` → `A MAN WITH A RAFT.`

segments.voice: A man comes to a wide river. No boat, no bridge. So he gathers grass, sticks, branches and leaves, ties them into a raft, and paddles across with his hands and feet. On the far shore he thinks: this raft was so useful. I'll lift it onto my head and carry it wherever I go. Would that be the right thing to do with a raft? the Buddha asks. No. Set it down on the shore, or let it float, and go on. In the sutta, the raft is the teaching itself: for crossing over, not for holding on to. Bringing it to a workday is a stretch, and an honest one. The work got you across the day. Thank it and set it down. A neighbor tradition says something close, in a different voice. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus says: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." That's what they share: the weight of work is real, and it isn't meant to ride on you forever. And here's the honest difference. In Matthew, rest is given: Christians hear Jesus offering it to whoever comes. In the raft story, nobody hands rest over. The one who crossed sees the raft has done its job, and sets it down. A gift received; a load released.
screen: `A RAFT OF GRASS AND STICKS.` · `ON THE FAR SHORE: SET IT DOWN.` · `MATTHEW: I WILL GIVE YOU REST.` · `REST GIVEN; A LOAD RELEASED.` · then, large: `PUT IT DOWN.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and rest your hands on your knees, closed gently, as if holding the day's work: the task, the email, the face. Then open your hands, palms up, and let it rest on the shore. Each time it climbs back on, open them again.
When work ends: the moment to set the raft down. It got you across, and you don't carry it home on your head.
Your line: put it down. The raft has done its job for today. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the raft simile to warn against clinging, even to the teaching, and some lay practitioners mark the end of a workday with a short sit or a few quiet breaths.

fork.setup: you got home an hour ago and you're still rewriting a message to your boss in your head. what would the man with the raft do?
options: thank the day for getting him across, and leave it on the shore.
keep it on his head; it was useful, so it might be again.

fork.reveal: the raft was good; that's why he's tempted to carry it. the Buddha's answer: set it on the shore and go on.

notes: MN 22 raft simile paraphrased (grass, sticks, branches, leaves; crossing with hands and feet; carrying it on his head vs setting it on dry land or in the water). The lesson says plainly that in the sutta the raft is the teaching itself, and applying it to a workday is a stretch. Confirm wording and framing.

Unity thread (wisdom day): shared, the weight of labor isn't meant to be carried forever (Matthew 11:28, KJV); honest difference, in Matthew rest is given by Jesus to whoever comes, while in the raft simile the one who crossed sets the load down. Ranks neither. A Christian reader and a Buddhist Keeper should both confirm the framing is fair.
